title: What payment-versus-payment could change for EUR/SGD funding
summary: The Deutsche Bundesbank and the Monetary Authority of Singapore demonstrated that two independently operated test ledgers could settle both sides of a EUR/SGD exchange to a common outcome. Each central bank retained control of its own ledger and settlement requirements. The economic question was whether an institution could obtain currency closer to the time it had to make a payment, while remaining protected against delivering its currency and receiving nothing in return. The experiment established the feasibility of coordinating the exchange. It did not measure a reduction in the amount or cost of funding (pp. 2–5).

Deutsche Bank and DBS participated as commercial banks, with Partior providing technology. Once payment instructions matched, euro and Singapore dollar tokens were locked on their respective ledgers. A cryptographic proof allowed each lock to be verified. One decision could then be recorded and proven to both ledgers so that the locked assets could be released. This dispensed with the need for a shared central bank ledger or a direct technical link between the two. It still required a party able to generate the proofs, access to the relevant ledger data and a means of relaying the proofs. Generating them accounted for most of the settlement time in the experiment (pp. 3, 5).

The first use case concerns an investor buying securities abroad. A shorter securities settlement cycle leaves less time between knowing the allocation and having the foreign currency available to pay for it. If FX could settle over a longer operating window, the investor or its bank might commit the currency later. The potential saving is the cost of prefunding cash or arranging credit before the precise need is known. The purchase still has to be funded by its deadline. The value of the proposed arrangement depends on how often the existing FX window forces cash to be held early (p. 4).

The second use case concerns a bank that is short of one currency for part of a day and expects to have a surplus later. An intraday FX swap could supply that currency and reverse the exchange once the shortfall passes. Matching the duration of funding to the duration of the payment need could reduce idle balances and their earnings drag. This is a narrower proposition than obtaining cheaper funding throughout the day. The note provides neither swap prices nor evidence of the availability of a willing counterparty at the necessary hour (p. 4).

Both examples depend on recognising when a payment is final and when the recipient can use its money. Technical verification establishes what a ledger recorded. The central banks would still have to determine how that outcome is recognised under the relevant legal frameworks and who governs access to the infrastructure. The authors identify wider European and Asia-Pacific connectivity as a possibility for further work. Their conclusions concern this bilateral experiment and two potential uses, with commercial performance and the operating arrangements for wider adoption still open (pp. 5–6).

questions.question: How often does the existing FX window actually force early funding?
questions.detail: The securities example locates a timing mismatch without measuring its frequency. Compare allocation times, FX value times, cash deadlines and committed credit lines for the same EUR/SGD securities purchases. Custodian settlement records and bank treasury logs could show whether the addressable cost arises routinely or mainly on exceptional days.

questions.question: Would the price of an intraday swap absorb the funding saving?
questions.detail: A bank might replace an unnecessarily long borrowing period with two shorter exchanges. The note gives no executable prices. Contemporaneous two-way dealer quotes, transaction fees and the costs of the existing facility would establish how much of the benefit reaches the institution supplying or receiving liquidity.

questions.question: At what point would a treasury desk count the proceeds as available cash?
questions.detail: The experiment verified locks and a common outcome, while legal recognition and dependence on proof services remain open. Scheme rules, jurisdiction-specific legal assessments and timed end-to-end recovery trials would help distinguish the moment principal is protected from the moment the recipient can meet another cash commitment.

limitation: The 16 November Insights Note reports a controlled proof of concept. Both commercial use cases are illustrative.
